steps.say: A line graph shows how one variable changes with another, such as temperature over time.
The variable you change goes on the horizontal axis. The variable you measure goes on the vertical axis.
Label both axes with units, and use even scales. Plot each point carefully, then join the points.
Look for a pattern, such as: the longer the time, the cooler the tea. Use it to estimate values between points.
An anomalous result does not fit the pattern. Check it by repeating the measurement.
Good evidence needs enough results. Two things rising together does not always mean one causes the other.

options.text: the first result in a table
options.why: The first result can fit the pattern perfectly well.

options.text: a result that does not fit the pattern

options.why: The biggest result can still fit the pattern.

options.text: a prediction made before the test
options.why: A prediction comes before any results.

hints: Most results in a good test follow a pattern.
One odd result can stand out from the rest.
Cross out the choices about order, size and predictions.
check.explanation: An anomalous result is one that does not fit the pattern of the others. It should be checked by repeating the measurement.

check.prompt: On a line graph of temperature against time, where does time go?

options.why: The vertical axis is for the variable you measure, the temperature.
The title names the graph. Time needs its own axis.
A key explains symbols or colours, not a variable.

hints: Time is the variable you choose when to measure.
The variable you measure goes up the side of the graph.
Cross out the parts of a graph that are not axes.
check.explanation: Time goes along the horizontal axis because it is the variable you choose. Temperature, which you measure, goes on the vertical axis.
